newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ill Yeltsin is still brave, power-hungry, loved.
newsitem.headline: Ill Yeltsin is still brave, power-hungry, loved.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's heart may be sick, but his mind and will seem undimmed.
It was classic Yeltsin -- bold in the face of danger, hungry for power, the beloved and loving family man -- who braved the uncertainty of open heart surgery, and came through it.
In trademark style, it took the the 65-year-old leader an age of hesitatation before deciding to go under the knife.
Some reports said it was Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, 58, who browbeat Yeltsin with his own experience of a bypass -- eight years ago -- into consenting to surgery.

But once the decision was made and announced on September 5, Yeltsin was determined to get it over with quickly so that he could "return to active life". He was clearly angry with doctors who insisted on a longer than expected preparation period.
"He suffers because he cannot work flat out, that is a full working day from morning to night," his wife Naina said in a television interview in late October.
"In general we do try to get him away from this but he practically never listens to anyone."
Yeltsin, clearly ill, made a huge effort from time to time to stay in charge and demonstrate it.

He summoned all his energy to go on national television on October 17 and, signing the order on-camera, sack former general Alexander Lebed as his top security aide, denouncing his open parade of presidential ambition.
Yeltsin did not change even in the hours before he was wheeled into the operating theatre.
His spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Tuesday that Yeltsin had combed his hair and dressed meticulously, chosing his best sweater before moving in to the hospital.
Asked by one of his family why he bothered, Yeltsin answered: "I am facing a very responsible day in my life."
Always at his best when facing a danger or threat, he smiled and joked with the doctors.
"Are you here with the knife already?" Yeltsin told the medical team who came to escort him to the clinic.

Yeltsin, a man who clearly relishes in power, tranferred his presidential authority to Chernomyrdin minutes before he went under the knife. But he took it back less than 24 hours later, the moment he woke up on Wednesday.
He immediately started badgering his doctors to move him from the heart hospital where he was operated on to another, clearly eager to show to the world the speed of his recovery.
This earned him clucking warnings from doctors, his wife and even from Chernomyrdin not to move too fast. But, judging by his history, warnings will not stop the born fighter from the Urals.
In his autobiography, Yeltsin recalls that as a student, he played volleyball for hours every day and studied at night.
The stress landed him in hospital, but he ignored doctors' warnings and discharged himself.
"The risk was colossal and I could have ruined my heart forever," he said, with a hint of dark prophesy.
Yeltsin is adored by his family. Naina, full of emotion shortly after the operation, told ORT television: "I would love to get a glimpse of him even with one eye."
A day later, visibly relieved after visiting Yeltsin with their two daughters, Naina told Russian television: "There is a totally different mood...you feel like smiling."
But, she added with a noted of exasperation, he was still too eager for his own good.
"We will really, really hold him back," she insisted.
